_doc: Freestyle fault taxonomy. Canonical machine-readable source, consumed by both the analysis layer and the web app. A fault belongs here ONLY if it is plausibly detectable from our realistic input: a single phone camera filmed poolside through moving water. Every entry is status=candidate until a detection method is proven on real footage. Each fault carries an `elite` reference — the standard a technically excellent swimmer meets. Assessment is scored as deviation from that reference, not as a present/absent judgement, because a model asked to judge defaults to a competent-club-swimmer baseline and reports nothing.

faults.name: Crossover entry
faults.short: Hand crosses the midline on entry
faults.why: Sends the body snaking, costs distance per stroke and adds drag. Very common in self-taught triathletes.
faults.detection: Wrist keypoint crosses the head-hip midline axis at entry.
faults.elite: Hand enters and extends within the shoulder line, never crossing the head-hip midline. Even 5-10cm of crossover is a deviation.

faults.name: Dropped elbow catch
faults.short: No early vertical forearm through the catch
faults.why: The single biggest propulsion loss in freestyle: the arm pushes water down rather than back.
faults.detection: Elbow-wrist-shoulder angle during the catch phase. Hardest of the set: the catch is underwater and refraction degrades keypoints.
faults.elite: Elbow stays high and forward of the wrist through the catch; forearm vertical by roughly 45 degrees of arm travel.

faults.name: Low elbow recovery
faults.short: Arm swings wide and flat on recovery
faults.why: Wide recovery forces counter-rotation and disrupts alignment; also a shoulder-injury risk over volume.
faults.detection: Elbow height relative to shoulder and wrist during the recovery arc.
faults.elite: Elbow is the highest point of the recovering arm throughout; hand stays inside the elbow line and close to the water. Any point where the hand is higher than the elbow is a deviation.

faults.name: Scissor kick
faults.short: Legs split laterally instead of kicking in line
faults.why: Large drag penalty. Usually a symptom of crossover or over-rotation rather than a root cause, so treat the cause too.
faults.detection: Lateral ankle separation relative to the body line.
faults.elite: Feet stay within the body's width, kick driven from the hip with a loose ankle. Any lateral separation beyond hip width is a deviation.

faults.name: Low body position
faults.why: Dominant fault in triathletes who train in wetsuits and lose the free flotation in the pool. Large drag cost.
faults.detection: Hip keypoint depth relative to the shoulder line. Likely the most reliably detectable fault in this set.
faults.elite: Hips and heels break or nearly break the surface; the body line is flat. Hips visibly below the shoulder line is a deviation, including if it only happens during the breath.

faults.name: Head too high
faults.why: Lifting the head drives the hips down; often the root cause of low body position.
faults.detection: Head-spine angle relative to horizontal during the non-breathing phase.
faults.elite: Waterline sits at the crown or upper forehead, eyes down or slightly forward. Any part of the forehead consistently clear of the water is a deviation.

faults.name: Insufficient rotation
faults.why: Flat swimming shortens the stroke and blocks the lat from contributing power.
faults.detection: Shoulder-line roll angle across the stroke cycle.
faults.elite: Shoulders roll roughly 45-60 degrees each side. Under 40 degrees is a deviation.

faults.name: Over-rotation
faults.why: Costs stroke rate and destabilises the kick; frequently produces a scissor kick downstream.
faults.detection: Peak shoulder-line roll angle per stroke.
faults.elite: Shoulders roll roughly 45-60 degrees each side. Beyond 60 degrees, or rotation that stalls the kick, is a deviation.

faults.name: Short finish
faults.short: Hand exits before passing the hip
faults.why: Throws away the most propulsive part of the stroke; shows up as low distance per stroke.
faults.detection: Wrist position at exit relative to the hip keypoint.
faults.elite: Hand accelerates past the hip, thumb brushing the thigh before exit. Exiting at or before the hip is a deviation.

faults.name: Lifting to breathe
faults.short: Head lifts rather than rotates for air
faults.why: Interrupts alignment every breath cycle. Especially costly in open water where breathing is frequent.
faults.detection: Vertical head displacement during the breath compared with the non-breathing baseline.
faults.elite: Head rotates with the body roll, one goggle stays in the water, no vertical lift and no pause in the stroke. Any vertical head rise is a deviation.
